claims.text: SECTION 2a PROVENANCE. Jacobs is the exception in this cluster and the reason the provenance test is worth applying. He published under his own name in the National Enquirer in 1982 and in the MUFON UFO Journal, No. 249, in January 1989, years before any interviewer sought him out, and was then answered by name and in print by a hostile participant who confirmed his unit, his appointment, his presence and his debriefing while disputing what he saw.

conflicts: The date. Jacobs's own 1989 article gives 2, 3 or 15 September 1964. Kingston George fixes the event at dawn on 22 September 1964, on an Atlas launch nicknamed 'Buzzing Bee', and cites a staff study he wrote on 13 October 1964. Both cannot be right and the board carries the discrepancy rather than resolving it.
The clearance. Jacobs's account depends on having seen and understood the product; George states in print that he was not authorised to view it and probably never gained the required clearance.

label: Robert M. Jacobs
narrative: Robert Jacobs is the one witness in this cluster whose claimed role is confirmed by an independent named participant, and the confirmation comes from the man who spent a published article demolishing his interpretation. He published his own account twelve years before the Disclosure Project existed, in the MUFON UFO Journal of January 1989, giving his post as Officer-in-Charge of Photo-optical Instrumentation in the 1369th Photographic Squadron at Vandenberg Air Force Base from May 1963 to May 1966. In 1993 Kingston A. George, who identifies himself in his opening line as the project engineer for the experiment, answered him in the Skeptical Inquirer, and in the course of doing so confirmed that Jacobs was named on-site commander by the 1369th Photo Squadron and managed the logistics at the Big Sur location, published photographs of the team and captioned Jacobs into and out of them, named the launch and gave its date, and cited a contemporaneous internal Air Force staff study by title and date. That is the rarest evidentiary shape on this board: two first-person published accounts by two people who were both there, agreeing about who was present and disagreeing about what the film showed. George's counter-explanation is that the imagery was decoy and chaff deployment, that the alarm which followed was about a classified weapons vulnerability rather than anything extraterrestrial, and that Jacobs was not cleared to interpret what he had seen. Jacobs's own dating is uncertain in his own article, which gives 2, 3 or 15 September 1964, while George fixes the event at dawn on 22 September 1964. The board should build this node on the 1989 publication and not on the Briefing Document, which arrived last and adds nothing but a date.
